name: Beaumont 'Beau' Fairchild
languages: French (from the Jesuits in Baltimore, who would be appalled at the use he makes of it)
equipment: A plum-coloured frock coat, a brocade waistcoat, a boiled shirt and a black string tie, all a little too good for Gilead and all slightly worn at the cuffs
Derringer (Remington over-and-under, .41), 2 rounds loaded, in a spring holster up his left sleeve
Boot knife in his right boot
Two decks of playing cards, one honest and one he would not show a friend
A faro dealing box, which he does not use in the Antelope out of respect for his partner
A deed for a one-third share in the Antelope Saloon, Gilead, won from Rufus Kemble on a full house in March
Sheriff Silas Quinlan's IOUs, $400 in all, in the sheriff's own hand, tied with a red ribbon
A gold-cased pocket watch engraved to someone called Thaddeus, which he won and never explains
A pearl-grey hat, a silk handkerchief, and a flask of good Kentucky whiskey that he never offers to anyone he is playing against
features: Book Learning (Back East origin: advantage on Investigation checks to read documents such as deeds, contracts, ledgers, telegrams and forged papers; once per long rest, recall one useful fact about a law, process, science or history without a check; disadvantage on the first Riding or Survival check in front of strangers each day)

Read the Table (Gambler: proficiency bonus doubled for Gambling and Insight checks; once per short or long rest, after a minute of watching or talking to a person, he learns one thing they are hiding: a lie, a weapon, the card they need, who they fear or what they want from him; he always knows whether a game is honest)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, an extra 1d6 damage to one creature he hits with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm if he has advantage, if another enemy of the target is within 5 ft of it, or if the target believed a bluff or lie he told within the last minute; not part of the damage on his sheet)

Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: 3 luck points, his CHA modifier, regained on a long rest; spend one to roll an extra d20 on an attack, check or save and choose which to use, or to make a creature within 30 ft reroll an attack against him)

Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: he draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action without anyone who isn't watching his hands noticing until he uses it, and has advantage on Sleight of Hand checks to carry one past a search or the marshal's gun check; on each of his turns he can take a bonus action to Dash, Disengage or Hide)

Know the Games (Card Sharp background: in any town he finds the best game, the crooked one and the man who runs both within an hour; he knows the house rules and house cheats of poker, faro, monte and chuck-a-luck, and when to leave town)

personality.traits: I talk beautifully, constantly, and about nothing, so that nobody notices what I am watching. I never cheat a poor man, a drunk or a friend. I tip everybody. I am always the best-dressed man in the room and I am always slightly in debt.
personality.ideals: Everybody is playing a hand. The only sin is playing it badly, or pretending you are not playing at all.
personality.bonds: My third of the Antelope, which is the first thing I have ever owned that I did not lose again by Tuesday. And, God help me, Silas Quinlan, who is the worst poker player in Wyoming and the only honest sheriff I have ever met.
personality.flaws: I cannot walk away from a game, a dare or a pretty woman's question. I hold the sheriff's IOUs, and I have not yet decided whether I hold them as a friend or as a weapon, which tells you everything about me.

appearance: A slim, elegant, dark-haired man of thirty-three with a narrow clever face, a pencil moustache, long white hands that are never still, and eyes the colour of weak tea that miss nothing. Plum coat, pearl-grey hat, a silk handkerchief, and the slightly worn magnificence of a man who has been rich and poor several times this year.
backstory: Beaumont Fairchild was the third son of a Baltimore shipping family that lost its ships in the panic of 1873 and its manners shortly after. He was educated by the Jesuits, apprenticed to a bank, dismissed from the bank, and discovered at twenty-one that he could remember every card in a deck and read every man at a table. He has played on Mississippi steamboats, in Denver's best hotels, in railroad camps from Omaha to Ogden and in a Leadville saloon from which he left by the window. He came to Gilead in January 1886 on the Rawlins stage because he heard that a new county seat full of cattlemen and lawyers would be good for business, and by March he had won a third of the Antelope Saloon from Rufus Kemble on a full house, queens over nines, and $400 in IOUs from Sheriff Silas Quinlan, who plays every Thursday and loses every Thursday. Cyrus Ballantine plays with him too, on the first Saturday of the month, and pays his losses in Company drafts. Beau likes Gilead more than he has liked anywhere, which worries him. When a homesteader is hanged at the Narrows and the street splits in two, he discovers that he owns a third of the saloon one side drinks in, holds the sheriff in his pocket, and plays cards with the Company's manager, and that every side now thinks he is on theirs. (Suggested employer: whoever bids highest, or the sheriff, as a favour. Hooks into both sides: the Antelope, the IOUs, and Ballantine's Saturday game.)
